analysis.one_liner: Caps speculator positions and forces transparency in energy and farm commodity markets.
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 2008 during the oil price spike with two cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or vote in the House Agriculture Committee and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: After oil prices hit record highs in 2008, this bill would have directed the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to set hard limits on how many contracts any one speculator can hold in energy and farm commodities, and to make big traders in opaque over-the-counter swaps report their positions. It also would have barred foreign exchanges from giving U.S.-based traders access to their screens for energy and farm contracts unless they published the same trading data and enforced comparable position limits as U.S. exchanges, and it would have added at least 100 staff to the CFTC for enforcement [S2] [S3]. The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Households paying gasoline, heating oil, and natural gas bills, and farmers and food buyers exposed to volatile commodity prices. Airlines and other businesses that buy fuel would also benefit if limits on speculators reduce price swings. Genuinely hedging firms keep an explicit exemption in the bill [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires the CFTC, within 60 days, to set limits on the number of positions any one person may hold in energy and agricultural commodity futures, including aggregate limits across all contract months and across other markets, to prevent excessive speculation, manipulation, and price distortion [S3].

Subjects over-the-counter swap transactions, index traders, and large traders to routine reporting and recordkeeping, and lets the CFTC impose position limits on over-the-counter contracts found capable of disrupting prices or liquidity [S2] [S3].

Closes the 'foreign board of trade' loophole: a foreign exchange cannot give U.S.-located participants direct access to trade energy or agricultural contracts that settle against U.S. prices unless it publishes comparable daily data and enforces comparable position limits [S3].
Directs the CFTC to publish weekly data separating index-fund and other passive positions from bona fide hedgers, so the public can see who is betting and who is hedging [S3].
Adds at least 100 full-time CFTC employees for transparency and enforcement, elevates the agency's Inspector General, and authorizes expedited procedures so the agency can act quickly [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Financial firms that take large speculative positions in commodity markets — swap dealers, index funds, and energy traders on U.S. and foreign exchanges — would face position caps, detailed reporting, and recordkeeping open to CFTC and Justice Department inspection. If speculators were a meaningful driver of 2008 prices, traders profiting from that activity would give up part of those profits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Swap dealers, index funds, energy traders

drawbacks.text: Economists disagreed sharply about whether speculators drove the 2008 price spike; the bill itself orders a GAO study of speculators' effects on prices, acknowledging the evidence was unsettled at the time it was written [S2] [S3].

Position limits can shrink market liquidity, which raises hedging costs for the airlines, farmers, and fuel buyers the bill is meant to help; the bill tries to manage this by protecting bona fide hedgers and directing the CFTC to preserve liquidity, but the tradeoff is real [S3].

The bill carries a provision shielding U.S.-registered traders from fraud liability for contracts traded on properly regulated foreign exchanges, weakening accountability on exactly the offshore venues it targets elsewhere [S3].
It leans on advisory groups of hedgers, traders, and exchanges to recommend the actual limit levels, which gives the affected industry a formal seat in setting the rules that bind it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If excessive speculation was inflating energy and food prices in 2008 — which was widely believed at the time but never definitively proven — position limits and transparency would have put real money back in consumers' pockets at a cost borne by big traders. Even if speculation was not the main driver, forcing foreign exchanges and over-the-counter dealers to disclose positions and take losses the same way U.S. exchanges do is a durable consumer safeguard. The bill's own safe harbor for foreign-exchange trades and its industry advisory groups are genuine weaknesses, and the liquidity cost of hard limits is not trivial. On balance a reasonable consumer-protection bill whose main value depended on facts still being debated.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or markup, and expired when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 18, 2008 — months after oil peaked near $147 a barrel that summer — and referred the same day to the House Committee on Agriculture [S1] [S5].
The sponsor made introductory remarks on the floor four days later, and the bill attracted two cosponsors [S4] [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action [S5].
The bill died at the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Swap dealers, commodity index funds, and the overseas exchanges that were selling U.S. traders access to energy contracts without U.S.-style limits kept operating unimpeded, and the CFTC never got the 100 new enforcement staff or the authority to cap positions across all markets.

for.name: Rep. Ellen Tauscher
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave floor remarks urging action on speculation in commodity markets.

for.name: Reps. Artur Davis and Carolyn McCarthy

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Collin Peterson (D-MN)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, markup, or vote for the final three and a half months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows the split; its sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and it died in a committee run by a fellow Democrat, so the obstacle was inaction rather than a partisan bloc.

industries.industry: Commodity swap dealers and index funds
industries.note: They would face hard position limits, routine detailed reporting of over-the-counter positions, and records open to CFTC and Justice Department inspection. Their profits depend on taking large positions in energy and farm markets that consumers ultimately buy from.

industries.industry: Foreign futures exchanges (e.g. overseas venues selling U.S. traders access to energy contracts)
industries.note: They would lose direct-access business from U.S.-located traders unless they published U.S.-comparable data and enforced U.S.-comparable position limits. During the 2008 spike these offshore venues let traders take positions in U.S. benchmark prices outside U.S. limits.

industries.industry: U.S. commodity exchanges and futures commission merchants
industries.note: They face new core-principle duties to set speculator position limits and reporting obligations, but they also lose business to offshore venues that would now be held to the same standards, leveling a competitive field they had conceded.

industries.industry: Bona fide physical hedgers (airlines, fuel distributors, grain firms)
industries.note: The bill keeps their hedging exemption and directs the CFTC to preserve liquidity for them while capping speculators; limits that curb price distortion make their fuel and crop costs more predictable.
